scenes.text: One night in 1986, seventeen hundred people in Cameroon died in their sleep. No fire. No lava. No sound.
By morning, whole villages were silent. Most victims had not a single wound.
The killer was a lake. Lake Nyos suddenly released a giant cloud of carbon dioxide. Invisible. Odorless. Heavier than air.
It poured down the valleys and smothered everyone in its path.
And it can happen again, at a lake much bigger than this one. Full story on Oddly Logical Science. Subscribe for more true stories this strange.

shorts.title: This lake works like a soda bottle.

scenes.text: This lake killed seventeen hundred people. And it works exactly like a soda bottle.
Deep down, the water holds huge amounts of carbon dioxide, trapped by pressure.
Disturb it, and the gas rushes out all at once.
In 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon did exactly that. One night. One burst. Seventeen hundred dead.
Today, pipes let the gas out slowly, so the bottle never pops again. Full story on Oddly Logical Science. Subscribe for more true stories this strange.

shorts.title: 2 million people live next to this lake.

scenes.text: Two million people live beside a lake full of dangerous gas.
Lake Kivu, between Congo and Rwanda, holds a huge amount of dissolved carbon dioxide and methane.
And it sits next to Nyiragongo, one of Africa's most active volcanoes.
In 1986, a much smaller lake in Cameroon released its gas and killed seventeen hundred people.
Scientists watch Kivu closely, and power plants now pull gas out of it. Full story on Oddly Logical Science. Subscribe for more true stories this strange.
